1.pericope_label: After Joshua: the oracle, Judah and Simeon, and Adoni-bezek

schools.summary: Gill explains that Simeon is called Judah's brother because the two were sons of the same father and mother, which was not true of all Jacob's sons, and because their possessions lay near together, Simeon's inheritance falling within Judah's; he has Adoni-bezek flee toward Jebus and be overtaken, and reads his speech as the words of a conscience accusing him and obliged to own that he was righteously dealt with.

Henry observes that Joshua left no successor in his own authority, so that the people had to consult the breastplate of judgment instead of a man, and gives four reasons for Judah's precedence: that the tribe was most numerous and powerful, that it was first in dignity and therefore first in duty, that it had been first served by the lot, and that Christ was to spring from it — drawing the rule that God appoints service according to the strength he has given, and that the burden of honour and the burden of work go together. On Adoni-bezek he reads the table literally and notes that the Israelites, while maiming him by the law of like for like, did not put him under it, which would have savoured of a haughtiness unbecoming an Israelite; and he makes the king's confession an instance of the power of conscience when God's judgments awaken it.

Clarke explains that shophetim are not judges in the usual sense but rulers with sovereign power who administer justice, make peace and war and lead armies, comparable to the Carthaginian suffetes, the Athenian archons and the Roman dictators, yet neither hereditary nor popularly chosen, so that the government was a theocracy and the judges God's deputies without pomp, state or emoluments; he calls the chronology of the book extremely embarrassed and the received method of reckoning the years of rest a violent perversion of the ordinary meaning of terms, and takes the author to be a single writer later than the period, most probably Samuel. He guesses only that the interval after Joshua's death was short, treats Adoni-bezek as a title, explains the mutilation as disabling a man for bow, sword and flight, gathers parallels from Aelian and Suetonius, derives the word poltroon from the Italian for a man without a thumb, and doubts that seventy kings ever literally fed under a table, taking the phrase for a proverb of the meanest servitude.

Keil and Delitzsch set out the plan of the book as an introduction, the history of the several judges, and a twofold appendix, and deny that Simeon is called brother because he and Judah shared a mother, pointing instead to Simeon's lot lying within Judah's territory. Ellicott presses the difficulty of the opening clause, arguing from the later report of Joshua's death and burial, from the improbability of inaction through a life of a hundred and ten years, and from the near-verbatim recurrence of these events in the previous book, that most of what follows preceded Joshua's death; he canvasses and rejects the proposed escapes, including the conjecture that a scribe wrote Joshua for Moses, and prefers to treat the sentence as a heading left standing when preface and appendix were added. He notes that the verb for consulting God here is a rare construction, takes it for inquiry by Urim and Thummim, reviews three theories of how those worked before concluding the truth is irrecoverable, observes that Judah camped eastward and marched first under a lion standard, and reports Simeon's fall from fifty-nine thousand fighting men to twenty-two between the censuses.

debates: Whether the chapter's events precede Joshua's death. Ellicott argues at length that they must, and treats the opening clause as a heading rather than a date; Clarke assumes the plain sense and supposes only a short interval, the enemy stirring once their champion was gone; Henry likewise takes it as written and builds on Joshua's having left no successor.

Why Simeon is called Judah's brother. Gill and Ellicott appeal to their being sons of the same mother, a thing not true of all Jacob's sons; Keil and Delitzsch expressly deny that this is the reason and refer the epithet to Simeon's inheritance lying inside Judah's territory.

Whether the seventy kings literally gathered food under Adoni-bezek's table. Clarke thinks it a proverbial expression for the meanest servitude and improbable as fact; Henry takes the table for real and draws a moral from the Israelites' refusal to use it against him.
outliers: Clarke's derivation of the English poltroon from an Italian word for a man whose thumb has been cut off.
Ellicott's conclusion that the working of the Urim and Thummim was forgotten thousands of years ago and will never be recovered.
Ellicott's report of Simeon's collapse from fifty-nine thousand fighting men to twenty-two thousand between the two censuses.
Clarke's verdict that the received chronology of Judges is a violent perversion of the ordinary meaning of terms.
themes: as I have done, so God has requited me

8.pericope_label: Jerusalem, Hebron and Debir, and the asking of Achsah

schools.summary: Gill reports the rabbis divided over whether Jerusalem was taken now or in Joshua's day, some referring the verse back and others urging that only Judah is named here where all Israel fought then and that Joshua's capture of the city is nowhere recorded, and he offers the compromise that the city was taken twice, the Jebusites having recovered it while Israel was occupied elsewhere; on Hebron he likewise treats the passage as a repetition of what was done under Joshua, while allowing the alternative that there were two distinct expeditions.

Henry dwells on Caleb's delay in taking possession of Hebron, which had been granted him a dozen years earlier by Joshua's own computation but was left unclaimed while he was employed in the public service he preferred to his private interest, so content was that good man to serve others and be served last.

Clarke reads the notice of Jerusalem as a parenthesis referring to the earlier capture under Joshua, and supposes that the Jebusites, discomfited then, had grown strong enough to repossess the city and afterwards to keep their stronghold on Mount Zion until the days of David; he describes Judah's territory as the most southern and very mountainous though with fine plains toward the west, and takes the whole section for a recapitulation of what the previous book had already related.

Ellicott objects that the English supplies the word had without warrant, as a gloss meant to push the conquest of Jerusalem backwards, and pieces the true account out of the earlier book, with the Jebusites left holding either citadel or town long enough for a later traveller to call it the city of a stranger; he distinguishes going up as the idiom for a campaign from going down for a particular battle, sorts the hill country, the dry south and the low maritime plain and assigns the chapter's towns among them, expounds Hebron's position and its older names, takes Sheshai, Ahiman and Talmai for clans of the Anakim and explains away the giant bones shown in Josephus's day as the remains of extinct animals, suggests that Kirjath-sepher, the city of the book, was a seat of Canaanite learning, raises the possibility that Caleb was of foreign origin, leaves the relation between Caleb and Othniel open between two constructions of the Hebrew, and reads Achsah's refusal to enter her husband's house, her leap from the ass and her request for the watered land as the acts of a woman more provident and less bashful than her husband. Keil and Delitzsch observe that Hebron and Debir have been described already, and that the word for spring stands here in a singular form.

debates: Whether Jerusalem was taken now or under Joshua. Clarke reads the verse as a parenthesis about the earlier capture; Ellicott calls the tense in the English an unwarranted interpolation and takes the action as present, with the Jebusites keeping the citadel; Gill lays out the rabbinic division and proposes that the city changed hands twice.

Whether the section repeats the previous book. Clarke, Gill and Keil and Delitzsch all treat Hebron and Debir as already narrated there; Gill alone keeps open the possibility of two separate expeditions rather than one account told twice.

What relation Othniel bore to Caleb. Ellicott shows that the Hebrew will support either that he was Caleb's brother, marrying his niece at a great age, or that Kenaz was Caleb's brother and Achsah his cousin, and notes that the Masoretic pointing takes the first.
outliers: Ellicott's explanation of the giant bones exhibited in Josephus's day as the remains of extinct animals mistaken for human ones.
Ellicott's suggestion that Kirjath-sepher, the city of the book, may have been a centre of Canaanite culture and learning.
Ellicott's suspicion that Caleb was of foreign origin, since a name meaning dog would be an unlikely one for a pure Israelite.
Henry's observation that Caleb, busy in the public service, was the last of his people to come into his own inheritance.
themes: a bride who would not go in

16.pericope_label: The Kenites, Hormah, the coast cities, and the iron chariots

schools.summary: Gill identifies the Kenites as the posterity of Jethro, noting that Jethro himself returned to his own country while Hobab and his descendants went with Israel into Canaan and settled in various parts, and that the family continued to the days of Jeremiah under the name of Rechabites; on the closing verses he records that the Targum reads the Word of the Lord where the text has the Lord, and that Gaza had fallen to Judah by lot but was not subdued until now.

Clarke follows Calmet in tracing the Kenites through the wilderness to a lot held with Judah and a residence in the city of palm trees during Joshua's lifetime, after which they moved south either from discontent with their portion or from molestation by the older inhabitants, and carries the line down to the Rechabites; he refers the destruction of Zephath to the transaction already recorded in Numbers; he sets out at length the Septuagint of the Vatican copy, which negates the capture of the Philistine cities, supports it from Augustine, Procopius and Josephus, and argues that the later history shows the towns in Philistine hands whether or not Judah briefly held them; and on the iron chariots he protests that they can hardly have been too strong for Omnipotence, holds the verse mistranslated, and follows the Chaldee paraphrast in referring the failure to a later time when Israel had sinned.

Ellicott identifies Jethro with Reuel, whose second name he takes for a priestly title in Midian, makes him the father of Zipporah and Hobab, and describes the Kenites as the elder branch of Midian, named from a chieftain Kain, dwelling among the rocks by the gulf of Akabah and originally cave-dwellers; he suggests that Jericho is called only the city of palm trees because its name lay under a curse, and that nomads would not have felt the scruple. He derives Hormah from the root of the ban and reads the conquest as the discharge of Israel's earlier vow; he reports the Septuagint negative on the Philistine cities while allowing that it may itself be a conjecture or a gloss, and calls the conquest very transitory; he observes that the Hebrew avoids saying Judah could not drive out the plain-dwellers and says rather that there was no driving out, so that the failure was of faith and not of power; he distinguishes the broad valley meant here from the coastal plain, doubts that scythed chariots existed so early, and disposes of the charge that the Kenites helped the enemy as resting on a Septuagint misreading of the word for chariot. He closes by noting that Judah nearly disappears from the rest of the book. Keil and Delitzsch place Zephath on the southern boundary and identify its ruins, and read the order of the Philistine cities as proof of an advance from the south, adding that all three were in Philistine hands again by Samson's time.

debates: Whether Judah really took the Philistine cities. Clarke prefers the Septuagint negative, backed by Augustine, Procopius and Josephus, and doubts the Hebrew as it stands; Ellicott reports the same reading but suspects the negative may itself be a conjecture inserted to remove a discrepancy; Keil and Delitzsch keep the Hebrew and limit the difficulty by making the tenure brief.

Why the plain could not be cleared. Clarke repunctuates the verse and imports from the Chaldee paraphrast the clause that it was afterwards, when they sinned, that the thing became impossible; Ellicott finds the answer in the Hebrew itself, which declines to say could not, and lays the failure to a faith cowed by the enemy's equipment.

Why the Kenites left the city of palm trees. Clarke offers discontent with their portion or molestation by the older inhabitants; Ellicott looks rather to the curse on the ruined city and to a Bedouin dislike of settled towns.
outliers: Ellicott's suggestion that Jericho goes unnamed here because a word under a curse was felt to carry a fatal force.
Clarke's exclamation that chariots of iron can hardly have been too strong for Omnipotence.
Ellicott's disposal of the old charge that the Kenites secretly aided the enemy, which rests only on the Septuagint reading the word for chariot as a proper name.
Ellicott's note that Judah all but disappears from the remainder of the book, producing no judge and going unmentioned in Deborah's song.
themes: a family that kept its tents

21.pericope_label: Benjamin and the Jebusites, and the taking of Bethel

schools.summary: Gill explains that neither Judah nor Benjamin, separately or together, could dislodge the Jebusites from the stronghold on Zion, which they held until David, and cites rabbis for whom Jerusalem was at this period not a walled city but a province divided between the two tribes and the Jebusites; on the fugitive from Bethel he holds that the land of the Hittites lay outside Canaan, supposing either that the people fled there when Joshua entered or that a colony of them had settled abroad earlier.

Henry remarks that Judah had set Benjamin a good example which Benjamin failed to follow for want of resolution; he supposes the tribal boundary ran through Bethel so that half belonged to each tribe, and that the vigour of the house of Joseph secured the whole of it. On the man who betrayed the entrance he declines to blame him if he acted from a conviction that the Lord was with Israel and the land theirs by grant, comparing Rahab's sheltering of her country's enemies who were God's friends, and declines equally to blame those who spared him, since one good turn requires another; but he notes that the man would not join himself to Israel, and that in naming his new city he kept Luz, an almond tree, in preference to Bethel, which carried religion in it.

Clarke concludes that the names of Judah and Benjamin must have been interchanged in one passage or the other, places the Jebusite stronghold in the northern part of the city that belonged to Benjamin, and infers from the writer's speaking of the Jebusites as still in possession that the book was composed before David's reign; he observes that Joshua took Ai but not Bethel, and reports that many manuscripts with the Septuagint and Arabic read children of Joseph for house of Joseph. On the informer he is unsparing, calling the conduct execrable and the man a traitor who bought his own life with the lives and property of his fellow citizens, and holding that the lawfulness of using such a man does not lessen the turpitude on his side; the land he fled to Clarke puts in Arabia, taking the man himself for a Hittite.

Ellicott assigns Jerusalem properly to Benjamin and explains its later attachment to Judah by David's capture of Zion, notes that the Jebusites remained tolerated inhabitants under a prince of their own and leave traces even after the exile, and infers from the assignment that the narrative is older than David's conquest; he accounts for Bethel's importance by its position on the highway between Hebron and Shechem and its associations with Abraham and Jacob, suspects that the tribal border may have divided the upper town from the lower, and remarks that the site is now a wretched village. Without moralising over the informer he observes that ancient armies could rarely storm a walled town and relied on blockade or betrayal, and compares the Persian capture of Sardis by a path discovered when a man climbed down after a fallen helmet. He places the new Luz toward the Phoenician frontier, reports a tradition of its purple dye, and notes that refounding a city under its old name was common, as when Teucer built a second Salamis in Cyprus. Keil and Delitzsch explain that what the man showed was not the gate but a way in, that the promise of favour covered his household, and that both the new Luz and the land of the Hittites are past locating, Hittites appearing at Hebron, in the hill country and far to the north-east at different periods.

debates: Whether the man who betrayed the entrance deserves blame. Henry excuses him on the analogy of Rahab, if he acted from conviction that the land was Israel's by grant, and excuses those who spared him; Clarke calls the conduct execrable whatever light it is viewed in, and holds that the lawfulness of using a traitor leaves his own turpitude untouched.

Why this verse assigns to Benjamin what the earlier book assigned to Judah. Clarke supposes the tribal names were interchanged in one passage or the other; Gill and Ellicott let the city straddle both lots, Gill on rabbinic authority making it a province rather than a walled town, Ellicott giving it properly to Benjamin.

What the phrase unto this day implies about the book's date. Clarke and Ellicott independently take it as evidence that the writing preceded David's capture of Zion, Ellicott adding that the narrative is nonetheless not contemporaneous with the events.
outliers: Ellicott's parallel of the Persians taking Sardis by following a man who had climbed down the hill fortress after a fallen helmet.
Henry's observation that the fugitive kept the old name Luz, an almond tree, in preference to Bethel, which carried religion in it.
Ellicott's report of a tradition that the second Luz was famous for its purple dye, and his parallel of Teucer founding a new Salamis in Cyprus.

27.pericope_label: The tribes that did not drive out

schools.summary: Gill supposes Ephraim's failure at Gezer to have been covered by a covenant made contrary to God's express command, observes that the two towns Zebulun left unsubdued had been assigned to the Levites, which may explain the sloth while aggravating the sin of not clearing cities given to religious persons, and reads the change of phrasing about Asher as meaning that the Canaanites were masters there and the tribe dwelt among them only on sufferance. On the mountain of Heres he takes the name for the sun and guesses either that the sun was worshipped there or that the mountain was named from the sun standing still near Aijalon.

Clarke notes that Beth-shean was the Scythopolis of the Greek version, reports the Septuagint's attempt to translate the local names into a mount of tiles where bears and foxes are, compares the driving of Dan into the hills with the Britons forced into the mountains of Wales by the Romans and the Indians pushed back into the woods by British settlers in America, and closes the chapter by remarking that few can be persuaded adversity is a blessing, though without it we should learn very little.

Ellicott traces the historian moving up the country from the southern tribes, grades each tribe's failure, marks the change of phrasing at Asher as the climax of degradation, and notes that Issachar is passed over altogether, suspecting the contented subjection in which that tribe bowed its shoulder to the yoke. Where Israel begins exacting tribute he inserts an excursus on the morality of the exterminating wars, arguing that nations must be judged by the standard of their own day, that the peoples of Canaan were practically irreclaimable and their neighbours would have learned their works, and that the Israelites acted from their better instincts, while insisting that the teaching of Christ has altered the world's moral conceptions and being severe on those who cite such commands to excuse later massacres. He identifies Beth-shean by the fastening of Saul's body to its wall and by its later name of contempt, derives Armageddon from Megiddo, calls the Amorites the highlanders of Palestine, and observes that the Amorites were made tributary to Ephraim rather than to the Dan they had displaced, so that the help given was at best somewhat selfish. Keil and Delitzsch argue that the serfdom of the Canaanites began gradually within the period of the judges and not as late as Solomon, follow Acco through its successive names to the Acre of the crusaders, and explain that Dan's allotment lay almost wholly in the plain, so that being forced into the hills excluded the tribe from its inheritance and drove part of it to emigrate.

debates: When Israel began exacting tribute instead of driving the Canaanites out. Keil and Delitzsch place it gradually within the period of the judges and argue expressly against a date as late as Solomon; Ellicott is less interested in the date than in the fact, which he treats as blameworthy and as the cause of the disasters that follow.

How the mountain of Heres and the towns beside it should be read. Gill takes the name for the sun and offers either local sun-worship or the miracle at Aijalon; Ellicott and Clarke report that the Greek translators read the consonants otherwise and got a mountain of potsherds, and turned the neighbouring names into a haunt of bears and foxes, the Hebrew words meaning gazelles and jackals.

What the closing note on the Amorite border is for. Ellicott offers either an explanation of Amorite stubbornness or a summary showing that only the southern frontier was ever made secure; on the rock named in it he and Keil and Delitzsch incline to Petra, though the identification is not agreed.
outliers: Ellicott's excursus arguing that the exterminating wars must be judged by the standard of their own age, with his warning against quoting them to excuse later massacres.
Clarke's comparison of Dan's fate with the Britons driven into the mountains of Wales and the Indians driven back by settlers in America.
Ellicott's observation that Issachar is passed over in silence, and his explanation from that tribe's contented subjection.
Ellicott's note that the Amorites were made tributary to Ephraim and not to the Dan they had displaced, which makes the rescue a selfish one.
themes: a tribe pushed into the hills
